content: Glycerin is a medication classified as a laxative and is approved by the FDA for the treatment of constipation. It is commonly associated with side effects such as rectal discomfort, a burning sensation, or diarrhea. Adult Indications and Dosage For adults, glycerin is indicated to relieve occasional constipation or irregularity. It typically induces a bowel movement within 15 minutes to 1 hour after administration. The recommended method of use involves inserting one suppository well into the rectum and retaining it for approximately 15 minutes. The suppository does not need to fully melt to exert its laxative effect. Pediatric Indications and Dosage For pediatric patients, glycerin is also indicated to relieve occasional constipation or irregularity. Similar to adults, it generally produces a bowel movement within 15 minutes to 1 hour. The administration involves inserting one suppository into the rectum and retaining it for 15 minutes, with no requirement for the suppository to melt completely to achieve its effect. Contraindications There is no specific information provided in the drug label regarding contraindications for glycerin. Warnings Glycerin is intended for rectal use only. It is not recommended to use laxative products for more than one week unless directed by a healthcare provider. Patients should consult a doctor before use if they experience stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, or a sudden change in bowel habits lasting more than two weeks. While using glycerin, some individuals may experience rectal discomfort or a burning sensation. If rectal bleeding occurs or if a bowel movement does not occur after use, the patient should discontinue use and consult a healthcare provider, as these symptoms may indicate a more serious condition. Adverse Reactions The most commonly reported adverse reactions include rectal discomfort, a burning sensation, and diarrhea. There is limited information available regarding adverse reactions observed during clinical trials or postmarketing surveillance. Drug Interactions There is no detailed information available regarding potential drug interactions with glycerin. Use in Specific Populations Pregnancy and Nursing Mothers: Pregnant or breastfeeding individuals should consult a healthcare professional before using glycerin. There is no specific guidance from the Australian Drug Evaluation Committee (ADEC) or the FDA regarding its use during pregnancy or breastfeeding. Pediatric Use: There is no specific FDA guidance on the use of glycerin in pediatric patients beyond the labeled indications. Geriatric Use: There is no specific FDA guidance on the use of glycerin in elderly patients. Gender, Race, Renal Impairment, Hepatic Impairment, and Immunocompromised Patients: There is no specific FDA guidance on the use of glycerin in these populations. Administration and Monitoring Glycerin is administered rectally. There is limited information available regarding specific monitoring requirements for patients using glycerin. Overdosage If glycerin is accidentally swallowed, medical assistance should be sought immediately, or a Poison Control Center should be contacted. Pharmacology The active ingredient in each suppository is 2.1 grams of glycerin (USP). Inactive ingredients include purified water, sodium hydroxide, and stearic acid. There is limited information available regarding the pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, and nonclinical toxicology of glycerin. Alcohol Interaction The interaction between alcohol and glycerin has not been established. Patients should consult their healthcare provider regarding the potential effects of consuming alcohol while using this medication. Brand Names Glycerin is marketed under the brand name GLYCERIN®. Additional Information There is limited information available regarding clinical studies, storage conditions, packaging, and patient counseling for glycerin. There is also no established information on drug shortages or look-alike drug names.
